title: Fearlessness, the ninth Guru's gift
hook: not being scared, and not being scary: the ninth Guru holds both in one line

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Guru Arjan: poet, builder, editor, martyr. Your line was poet and builder. What did you tend, for someone else to stand in? Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

Which is harder: not being scared, or not being scary? It is easy to practice one and forget the other. Some people get brave, and somewhere on the way they get loud, sharp, a little frightening to the people around them. Others work so hard at being gentle that they never stand up to anything. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, puts both in a single short verse, near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib. Today we open the gift Sikhs remember him for: fearlessness, the kind with two halves.
screen: `NOT SCARED, OR NOT SCARY?` → `BRAVE AND SHARP, OR GENTLE AND SILENT.` → `ONE SHORT VERSE, TWO HALVES.`

segments.voice: The verse is one of his saloks, paraphrased. One who frightens no one, and who fears no one else: listen, O my mind, says Nanak, call that one wise. The ninth Guru signs as Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth. Notice the order. Frightening no one comes first. Fearlessness, in this verse, isn't a warrior's swagger. It starts with the people around you being safe with you. Now go back to the very beginning of the Granth, to the Mul Mantar, the root verse at its opening. Among the words it uses for the One are nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, and without enmity. The two sit side by side. The ninth Guru's salok takes those two qualities of God and sets them inside a human being. Without fear, you don't bow to threats. Without enmity, you don't make threats. They hold each other up. Here's why they belong together on an ordinary day. A lot of frightening comes from being frightened. The boss who shouts is sometimes afraid of looking weak. The kid who bullies is sometimes scared at home. And fear can make us small enough to stand by while others are frightened. Cut one root, and the other weakens. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur living this line to the end, standing firm under pressure, without hatred for those applying it. We'll come to that story in a couple of days. For now, just the line. Two halves. Neither fear nor frighten.
screen: `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `FRIGHTENING NO ONE COMES FIRST.` · `NIRBHAU AND NIRVAIR, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FEAR MAKES PEOPLE FRIGHTENING.` · then, large: `NEITHER FEAR NOR FRIGHTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle and brave. Settle, and breathe. First, bring to mind one person who might be a little afraid of you. A child, someone who reports to you, a younger sibling, a waiter. Breathe out, and soften toward them. Then bring to mind one thing you've been afraid to say or do. Breathe in, and let your back straighten. Go back and forth: soft toward them, steady toward it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru, without fear and without enmity, on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Fearlessness. In the ninth Guru's salok, the wise one frightens no one and fears no one, both halves together. Today's word.
Your line: neither fear nor frighten. Today, do the brave thing you found, and do it gently enough that nobody around you has to flinch. Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: The saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur are read near the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs quote this verse on fearing no one and frightening no one when they speak of his life.

fork.setup: you've finally found the courage to stand up to someone. the adrenaline is high. how do you speak?
options: loud and sharp, so they know you mean it.
steady and gentle, without frightening anyone.

fork.reveal: the ninth Guru's salok calls wise the one who fears no one and frightens no one. courage without menace.

original.note: without fear; a word for the One in the Mul Mantar, set beside nirvair, without enmity.

trapdoor: what you thought: fearlessness means not being scared.
what it means: fearing no one and frightening no one, both together.
what a scholar hears: the salok takes nirbhau and nirvair, words for the One in the Mul Mantar, and sets them inside a human life.
